title: Birch House
headline:
A kitchen with room
for everyday life.
problem: The original kitchen had plenty of floor area but very little generosity. An oversized run of upper cabinets interrupted the garden outlook. The island offered preparation space but made gathering awkward, and the tiled floor divided the room from the rest of the house. The brief was not simply to replace the cabinets. It was to make cooking, homework, arriving home and a long Sunday lunch feel equally natural in one space. The owners’ fictional priorities were practical: clear circulation, useful storage and a place to sit that did not block the person preparing dinner.
decision: We kept the room’s existing shell and garden-facing openings. That allowed the proposal to focus on circulation, joinery and light rather than extending the footprint. A longer working island holds the sink, preparation area and discreet storage, while a quieter rear elevation removes visual clutter. Three counter seats face the cook without occupying the main route through the room. A continuous oak floor brings the kitchen back into the life of the house. Tall storage is concentrated in one part of the elevation, leaving the rest lower and more open. Each decision supports the same goal: a room that works when it is full of people, not only when it is empty.
materialsText: Quarter-sawn oak is used where hands and eyes spend time: cabinet fronts, counter stools and open shelving. Honed limestone adds weight to the island without the glare of a polished surface. Aged brass introduces a small, warm contrast rather than a decorative theme. Limewash softens the remaining walls. The palette is deliberately limited, allowing grain, texture and daylight to do the work. A real specification would confirm stone sealing, coating durability and appliance clearances through samples and detailed drawings before fabrication.
stages: Survey and opening-up: confirm services, floor build-up and the condition behind existing joinery before ordering bespoke work.
First fix: coordinate plumbing, extraction and electrical routes with the final cabinet drawings; approve a full-size junction sample.
Installation: level the substrate, lay the continuous floor, fit joinery, template stone, then install fixtures and lighting.
Handover: test appliances and ventilation, adjust doors, record care instructions and review the room in daylight and evening lighting.
result: The proposed room feels more generous without gaining a square foot. The garden becomes part of the interior, the main route stays clear while someone cooks, and materials are arranged to age together. In this fictional study, success is practical: two people should be able to prepare a meal while another sits at the island, without negotiating a bottleneck. The matched images preserve the camera and architectural shell so the design changes can be compared directly. This is a concept proposal, not a completed client renovation or a measured performance claim.

title: Tidal House
headline:
Closer to the garden.
Still unmistakably home.
problem: An ageing conservatory at the back of the house was neither a comfortable living space nor a useful threshold to the garden. Its shallow roof restricted light in the original rooms, while the small openings made the outdoor space feel remote. The owners’ fictional brief asked for somewhere to gather throughout the year, but specifically avoided turning the house into an entirely different building. The addition needed to earn its footprint by improving the rooms already there, not merely providing another place to put furniture.
decision: The proposal replaces the conservatory with a carefully proportioned low extension. A continuous roof line establishes a calm horizontal datum below the existing pitched roof. Slender garden-facing glazing keeps the new volume visually light, while a solid cedar side wall provides privacy and a useful backdrop. The original house remains legible rather than disappearing behind the addition. A dining table is positioned to share light with the existing interior, and the terrace is designed as part of the same sequence. The layout is tested with chairs pulled out and people moving through the room, not just with furniture arranged for a photograph.
materialsText: Cedar and dark frames distinguish the new work from the limewashed house without a harsh contrast. Limestone paving extends warm mineral tones into the garden. Oak furniture introduces a domestic scale beneath the broad glazing. The roof edge is restrained, but its drainage, flashing and insulation must be resolved as carefully as the visible fascia. Material choices are connected to exposure, maintenance and the experience of crossing the threshold. The conceptual palette does not replace a site-specific envelope specification or thermal assessment.
stages: Measured survey and planning: establish boundaries, levels, drainage runs and the relationship between the new roof and existing openings.
Groundworks and structure: verify soil assumptions, coordinate foundations with existing services and establish weather protection before opening the house.
Envelope: complete the roof, insulation, glazing and drainage; inspect critical junctions before finishes conceal them.
Interior and landscape: complete services and joinery, establish properly drained thresholds, then finish the terrace and planting.
result: The design gives the house a new gathering room while preserving its original silhouette. The extension is not treated as an isolated glass box: structure, furniture, thresholds and garden are considered together. The paired visualisations use the same camera to show a conservatory being replaced, rather than comparing unrelated buildings. Foundation design, energy performance, permissions and contractor pricing would require professional investigation of a real site. No such approvals or completed construction are claimed. The value of this fictional study is the clarity of the proposed relationship between old and new.

title: Alder House
headline:
Less compartmentalised.
More connected.
problem: A sequence of individually reasonable alterations had left the fictional house feeling fragmented. Different floor finishes marked every threshold, furniture competed with circulation, and a partial division in the living room interrupted the garden view. The owners did not want an open-plan interior at any cost. They wanted rooms that felt connected while retaining places to read, talk and be alone. The challenge was to establish continuity without making every room identical or removing the character that had drawn them to the house.
decision: The whole-home proposal begins with the living room because it establishes the wider principles. Removing a redundant internal division makes the existing daylight useful across more of the plan. A lower furniture arrangement defines the sitting area without erecting another barrier. The hearth becomes a quiet anchor, with storage and circulation arranged around it rather than in front of it. Throughout the imagined house, thresholds are reduced to a small family of repeated details. The approach is selective: retain elements that contribute to daily life, remove those that obstruct it, and avoid changing sound fabric simply for visual consistency.
materialsText: Natural linen, oak, limewash and honed stone create continuity without uniformity. Linen is selected for visual softness, with upholstery durability and cleanability to be agreed during detailed design. The fireplace surround avoids elaborate trim and depends instead on proportion, reveal depth and the meeting of plaster with stone. A restrained oak frame and textured artwork bring a domestic scale to the tall wall. Grain, weave and shadow provide variation within a limited palette. Real samples would be reviewed together, including the way different materials meet at corners and thresholds.
stages: Whole-house audit: map structure, ventilation, electrical capacity and water services before deciding which rooms can be renovated independently.
Enabling work: protect retained elements, establish dust separation and agree any period of occupation during construction.
Coordinated first fix: resolve heating, lighting, power and ventilation with the furniture plan rather than after plastering.
Room-by-room completion: inspect junctions, commission services and document maintenance before the final defects review.
result: The living room demonstrates a broader whole-home strategy rather than pretending to show every affected space. Its measure of success is a calmer daily sequence: entering, putting things away, sitting down and moving towards the garden no longer compete for the same narrow route. The proposal retains the character of the house while making its rooms easier to use. The complete programme and cost would depend on surveys and an agreed phasing plan. This case study is a fictional design exercise, with matched architectural visualisations rather than photographs of a completed commission.

title: Orchard House
headline:
A little colour.
A lot of consideration.
problem: The existing kitchen’s dark laminate fronts and tiled floor absorbed light and made a generous room feel crowded. The fictional owners wanted a kitchen that could tolerate family activity without looking utilitarian. Their priorities were more useful storage, better sightlines to the garden and somewhere to sit that did not block the working area. They liked colour but did not want a room that depended on a fashionable finish to feel complete. The layout, surfaces and lighting had to work as a single proposal.
decision: Tall storage is separated from the principal preparation zone. A central island provides the everyday working surface, while the rear run becomes a quieter elevation with a small shelf rather than a wall of upper cabinets. Grey-olive lacquer gives the lower joinery a distinct identity, balanced by oak in the taller elements. The arrangement creates a hierarchy: durable surfaces where work happens, warmer materials where people gather, and clear space where the eye meets the garden. Appliance positions and door swings are considered alongside the visible composition, so storage does not become an obstacle when the room is in use.
materialsText: The olive finish is muted enough to sit beside planting but substantial enough to distinguish this scheme from Birch House. Pale limestone keeps the work surface calm. Brass is restricted to touchpoints and the mixer rather than repeated as decoration. Oak stools, shelves and floorboards introduce related but different grain directions. Finish samples would be reviewed together in the actual room: a colour seen under studio lighting cannot be assumed to match coastal daylight. The lacquer system, stone protection and hardware specification would be confirmed before fabrication.
stages: Brief and sampling: test the palette alongside retained architecture, then confirm appliance sizes and storage requirements.
Technical coordination: agree extraction, sockets, water isolation and the sink detail before approving joinery drawings.
Fabrication and installation: inspect the lacquer sample, set the cabinet datum, fit the island and template stone from installed joinery.
Completion: commission appliances, check worktop lighting, adjust hardware and leave a maintenance guide for every finish.
result: The study shows how restrained colour can support a room’s organisation rather than decorate it afterwards. The island has a working side and a gathering side, while the existing windows remain the dominant architectural feature. Both comparison images share the geometry and lens, making the changes visible without a misleading viewpoint. This is a fictional proposal: no completed contract, client testimonial or measured performance claim is attached to it. A real project would translate the concept into coordinated drawings, samples and an agreed scope before construction began.

title: Courtyard House
headline:
An extra room.
A different relationship.
problem: The original conservatory occupied the right part of the garden but did little to improve the house. Its lightweight roof and fragmented frames made the connection feel temporary. The fictional brief asked for a room that could host an ordinary evening as comfortably as a larger gathering, while protecting privacy towards the neighbouring garden. Simply replacing the glazing would not address the relationship between the interior, the terrace and the remaining outdoor space. The project needed a clearer idea of where enclosure should end and the garden should begin.
decision: A solid cedar flank and a generous glazed face establish a deliberate balance between privacy and openness. The room is oriented towards a defined terrace rather than a leftover patch of lawn. Its roof sits below the existing house, maintaining a distinction between old and new. Furniture is used to test the footprint early: the extension must work with chairs pulled out and people moving through it. The terrace gives the room an outdoor counterpart, while planting softens the boundary beyond. The design avoids using glazing indiscriminately; a solid wall can make the remaining view more valuable.
materialsText: Deeper cedar tones give the courtyard room a more sheltered character than the Tidal House study. Dark frames reduce interruption across the garden elevation. Limestone pavers establish an orderly foreground, with softer planting beyond their edge. The contrast is intentional: a precise threshold followed by a less formal garden. A real specification would account for exposure, drainage and maintenance, particularly where timber sits close to planted ground. Roof junctions and thresholds would be developed as technical details rather than left to be improvised on site.
stages: Site and neighbour review: confirm boundaries, overlooking, construction access and the daylight implications of the new roof.
Enabling and groundworks: agree a protected route through the occupied property and inspect existing foundations before final structural decisions.
Structure and enclosure: install frame, roof and glazing with attention to movement joints and the old-to-new connection.
Fit-out and garden: complete lighting and services, test threshold drainage and finish the terrace before establishing planting.
result: The proposed extension is modest in area but changes the way the garden is used. It creates a place to gather at the edge of the house rather than a room that merely looks outward. The lower camera in this paired study emphasises roof line, terrace and planting, and is retained in both states. Permissions, structural design, thermal assessment and contractor pricing remain site-specific tasks; visualisation does not replace them. This fictional case study records a design intention, not a claim that the proposal has been built or professionally approved.

title: Harbour House
headline:
Calm, without
losing its character.
problem: The fictional house had generous windows and a good relationship with its site, but the interior arrangement did not make the most of either. A partial partition interrupted the living space, darker finishes dominated the lower half of the room, and seating left the most useful garden-facing corner underused. The owners wanted continuity across the house without removing every sign of its history. Their brief called for a calmer arrangement rather than a wholesale change in personality, with a practical plan for services and construction phasing behind the visible finishes.
decision: The living room becomes the centre of a wider sequence of spaces. The redundant division is removed, seating is brought into a conversational arrangement, and the hearth is simplified into a mineral surface rather than a decorative feature. The garden remains visible from several positions, including the main circulation route. Across the whole-home study, the same principles guide the work: retain what contributes, remove what obstructs, and make new details legible without making them loud. Lighting and furniture are considered together so the room can support reading, conversation and movement without a single dominant arrangement.
materialsText: Slate-toned linen gives this scheme a cooler coastal note while warm oak and pale stone prevent austerity. The contrast is concentrated in upholstery rather than spread across many finishes. A woven rug defines the sitting area and softens the acoustic character suggested by the hard surfaces. Limewashed walls and restrained joinery keep attention on proportion and daylight. The final textile and coating specifications would be selected for real household use, including cleaning, wear and repair. Samples would be checked in the room before the palette was applied throughout the house.
stages: Survey and priorities: record existing fabric, identify services needing upgrades and rank rooms by their effect on daily life.
Phasing and protection: decide whether occupation is practical, establish safe access and protect retained windows, floors and joinery.
Construction and coordination: complete structural changes and service upgrades before installing repeated finish details room by room.
Commissioning and handover: test systems, review snagging in different lighting and provide a room-specific maintenance record.
result: The illustrated result is quieter and more coherent while remaining domestic. The scheme gives the existing architecture and a few well-proportioned pieces more room to work, rather than filling every surface. Before-and-after images retain the camera, shell and garden relationship. As with every NORTHLINE study, this is an original fictional proposal rather than completed client work, and the whole-home scope extends beyond the one room visualised. A real commission would require measured information, technical coordination and a transparent agreement on scope and programme before the concept could become a building project.
